Fadeth
FADE-eth
v. (3rd pers. sing.)
The third-person singular present of fade, from Old French fader, to wither, from Latin fatuus in its sense of insipid or faded. Webster 1828: loseth colour or freshness; withereth; declineth. Scripture uses it of grass, flowers, our righteousnesses, and by contrast of what does not fade.

Biblical Definition

Fadeth is Scripture’s word for the short life of everything under the sun, and it is used to throw the imperishable into relief. Isaiah sets the two next to each other in a verse the New Testament quotes twice: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass (Isaiah 40:7), and the next verse answers, but the word of our God shall stand for ever. The fading is not accidental decay; the breath of the LORD does it. Isaiah applies the same word to the whole created order under judgment: The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish (Isaiah 24:4). James turns it on the rich man specifically, who withers in the middle of his pursuits: the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11). And Peter uses the negative form twice for what God keeps: an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4), and for the faithful elder a crown of glory that fadeth not away (1 Peter 5:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives FADETH as the third person singular of FADE: to lose colour; to lose freshness or vigour; to wither, as a plant; to decay; to vanish; to perish gradually.

FADETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb FADE.

FADE, v.i. — To lose colour; to lose freshness or brightness; to become faint in hue.

To wither, as a plant; to decay; to lose vigour or strength.

To vanish; to disappear gradually; as, the sound or the vision fadeth away.

From Old French fader, allied to Latin vado, to go, and to the English vade, an older form of the same word.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:7 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass."

Isaiah 24:4 — "The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish."

James 1:11 — "For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways."

1 Peter 1:4 — "To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,"

1 Peter 5:4 — "And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away."

Modern Corruption

A culture organised around the postponement and concealment of decline has no category for Isaiah 40:7, where the fading of human life is not a problem to be solved but the work of God’s own breath, done so that His word may be seen to stand.

expand to see more

Isaiah does not say the flower fades because of unfortunate conditions. He says the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it. The transience of human strength, beauty, reputation and life is a divine act with a stated purpose, and the purpose is announced in the next breath: the word of our God shall stand for ever. Against this, the modern project treats ageing as a defect to be corrected, death as a medical failure, and the reminder of either as morbid. The result is not that people fear death less but that they meet it unprepared and alone, having been promised by everything around them that the subject would not come up. Scripture’s counsel is the opposite: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom (Psalm 90:12).

James 1:11 names the specific form the illusion takes for the prosperous: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways — not after his ways, but in the middle of them, with the plans still running. And 1 Peter supplies the only genuine answer, which is not a longer flowering but a different kind of thing altogether: an inheritance that fadeth not away, kept somewhere the moth and the market cannot reach it, and a crown that does not wilt, given by the chief Shepherd to men who shepherded His flock without being lords over it. The believer is not asked to deny that he is grass. He is asked to place his hope in the word that outlasts the grass.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nabel (H5034), to wither, to fall away, to fade; yabesh (H3001), to dry up; Greek amarantos (G263), unfading, whence the amaranth flower; maraino (G3133), to wither, to fade away.

expand to see more

Hebrew nabel (H5034) — to fade, to wither, to fall; the flower fadeth (Isaiah 40:7) and we all do fade as a leaf (Isaiah 64:6).

Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up, to wither; the companion verb of nabel in Isaiah’s grass-and-flower figure.

Greek maraino (G3133) — to quench, to wither, to fade away; shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11).

Greek amarantos (G263) — unfading; the inheritance of 1 Peter 1:4, named from a flower the ancients believed never withered.

Greek amarantinos (G262) — of unfading quality; the crown of glory in 1 Peter 5:4.

Usage

"The grass withereth, the flower fadeth (Isaiah 40:7) — and the reason given is the breath of the LORD."

"So also shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11) — in the middle of his plans, not after them."

"An inheritance… that fadeth not away (1 Peter 1:4) — the only answer to the fading is a different kind of thing."
